paragraphs.text: An implementation MAY verify a subnet **in isolation**, its ports played by the environment, against a **contract** stating what the environment does and what the subnet guarantees. A net built from a fixed vocabulary of subnets is then proven one subnet at a time, each proof costing what the subnet costs rather than what the composed net's interleavings cost; the composition argument stays with the caller. Unlike [MOD-051], which wraps a subnet in environment places and checks each property separately, the contract is judged whole, over a closed net whose environment runs dry.
**The contract.**

- *Initial marking*: the tokens the subnet holds before anything arrives: its own resources and any shared pool it borrows from.
- *Arrival groups*: each delivers between `min` and `max` tokens in total, each onto one of its places, at any point of the run. Both bounds are finite: a bound is both the runtime cap and the width of the claim.
- *Count clauses*, each named: at every quiescent marking the tokens across the clause's places, each place counted once, number between `min` and `max`, or at least `min` for a clause with no `max`.
- *Rest places*: may hold any number of tokens at quiescence.
- *Designed terminals*: while a terminal's marker holds a token, clause lower bounds are waived (upper bounds are not) and the terminal's excused places may hold tokens. The marker itself may always rest, as in [VER-014].
- *Environment transitions*: fired by the environment, for a neighbour that reacts to what the subnet sends — a tool answering a request, a loop body sending an item back within a budget of its own — which an arrival group cannot express because its tokens do not wait for a request. A place only environment transitions touch is an **environment place**, the environment's own state; a place they share with the subnet is a port.
- *Termination*: no run fires forever, unless the contract waives it. A cycle of reapable transitions ([TIME-013]) counts too, since a run need not reap them.

A quiescent marking **meets** the contract when every clause holds, lower bounds only while no terminal marker is marked, and every token lies on a clause place, a rest place, an environment place, a terminal marker, or an excused place of a marked terminal. The second condition is the rest set of [VER-014] with the clause, rest and environment places as sinks and each terminal as a conditional sink, and implementations MUST decide it through that same predicate. Every other place is internal to the subnet and must be empty.

The verifier *shall* judge a quiescent marking to meet the contract exactly when, counting each place of a clause once, the tokens across each clause's places number at most the clause's `max` if it has one, at least its `min` unless some terminal marker is marked, and no marked place is stranded under the rest set of [VER-014] whose sinks are the clause, rest and environment places and whose conditional sinks are the terminals.

**Closure.** The subnet is verified as a closed net. Arrival group `i` contributes a source place holding `min` tokens and a source place holding `max − min`, each left out with its transitions when its count is 0, one transition per source and target place moving a token from that source onto the place, and a transition with no output that declines a token of the second source. A run is therefore quiescent only once every required arrival has happened and every optional one has been delivered or declined. The sources are ordinary places, not the environment places of [VER-006], which never run dry and would make every quiescence property hold vacuously.

The contract's environment transitions join the closed net unchanged. Their actions never run, so one that declares outputs gets a placeholder action instead of a [CORE-043] refusal. Contract places no arc touches join as places of their own and are listed in the report, so a clause over a place nothing writes counts zero there: a finding, never a refusal. The closure's names (`env:arrivals[i]`, `env:optional[i]`, `env:arrive[i]:<place>`, `env:arrive?[i]:<place>`, `env:decline[i]`) and the environment transitions' names MUST NOT collide with the subnet's, and a collision is refused. The in-flight split of [VER-004] applies to the closed net before the terminal rewrite of [EXEC-042]: the environment transitions stay atomic and their arcs count as tests, and a closed net the split refuses, or one that a declared mint transition ([NU-010]) is not in, is `Unknown` before either route runs.

*If* a name the closure adds, or the name of an environment transition, is already a place or transition name of the subnet, *then* the verifier *shall* refuse the closure, and it *shall* not refuse a closure whose added and environment-transition names are distinct from each other, from the subnet's names and from the environment places.

The verifier *shall* build the closed net from the subnet's transitions, then the environment transitions unchanged, then, for each arrival group `i` in order, numbered from 0, one immediate transition `env:arrive[i]:<place>` per target place, in the group's order, taking one token from the source `env:arrivals[i]` when `min > 0`, and one immediate transition `env:arrive?[i]:<place>` per target place, in the group's order, taking one token from the source `env:optional[i]`, followed by an immediate `env:decline[i]` discarding one, when `max > min`; the transitions the closure adds have no other arc.
The verifier *shall* start the closed net from the contract's initial marking with `min` tokens on `env:arrivals[i]` and `max − min` tokens on `env:optional[i]` for each source it builds.

The verifier *shall* treat as an environment place exactly a place that an environment transition touches and the subnet does not, and *shall* make every place of the subnet and every place the contract names a place of the closed net.
The verifier *shall* mark as environment steps exactly the environment transitions and the transitions the closure adds.
**Routes.** Both decide the untimed claim of [VER-004].

1. *Graph.* The closed net's state-class graph is built **untimed**: every clock gets the interval of `immediate()`, so the graph holds exactly the markings the untimed encoders reason about, even for a subnet with timed transitions. When the graph closes within the class budget the verdict is exact: every class with no enabled transition is judged, and a reachable cycle is a run that never comes to rest. When it does not close, a violation among the explored classes is still real, since a class with no enabled transition is quiescent whether or not it was expanded and a cycle among explored edges is a real cycle; only the absence of violations needs the graph to close.

The graph route MUST NOT run on a closed net that declares **match (ν-join) transitions**, the exclusion of [VER-017] condition 1. The graph is name-blind: it fires a join on tokens whose names differ, so it reaches markings the net cannot (the join's output) and misses quiescent markings the net reaches (the inputs of a join that never matches), and neither its `proven` nor its `violated` can stand. Such a net goes to the SMT route, whose pipeline has exact routes for a ν-net ([VER-012]), and the report says why the graph was skipped.
The flat encoders ignore timing; a ν-net's exact route ([VER-012]) does not, and on the timed net would decide the weaker timed claim.

Both routes read quiescence as [VER-002] does: a class or marking whose enabled transitions are all reapable ([TIME-013]) rests too. The reapable transitions are named on the closed net before the SMT route makes every transition `immediate()`. The option `assumeNoReaping` restores the plain reading, and the report of a closed net with a reapable transition says which reading the verdict used.
**Verdict.**

- `Proven`: every reachable quiescent marking of the closed net meets the contract and, where termination is required, no run fires forever.
- `Violated`: lists every broken part the deciding route found (each clause by name, each stranded place by name, and termination), each with a witness. A witness carries the firing sequence from the initial marking, environment steps included, the markings along it, and the **port trace**: the firings that touch a port or are environment steps (arrivals, declines and environment transitions), each marked as such, with the token changes on contract places and on the places environment transitions touch. On the graph route a witness is a shortest one, and a termination witness is a lasso that marks where its cycle starts. On the SMT route it is the deciding query's counterexample, which need not be shortest; one that does not replay as an ordered firing sequence ([VER-003]) is marked unconfirmed and names no stranded place.
- `Unknown`: says which parts no route decided, and why.
*If* the verifier refuses the closure, *then* it *shall* refuse the verification.

*When* the verifier accepts the closure, it *shall* return a result, and that result *shall* be `Proven` when the closed net declares no match transition, its graph closes within a class budget above 0, every reachable quiescent marking meets the contract and, where termination is required, no run fires forever.

The verifier *shall* return `Proven` only when every quiescent marking reachable in the closed net from its initial marking meets the contract, reading quiescence as [VER-002] does, or, when `assumeNoReaping` is set, as a marking with no enabled transition, and, where termination is required, no run of the closed net fires forever.

*When* the verdict is `Violated`, the verifier *shall* list at least one broken part, and for each part with a confirmed witness *shall* report a firing sequence of the closed net from its initial marking, environment steps included, that leads to a quiescent marking at which the named clause fails, or to a quiescent marking at which each named place, at least one, holds a stranded token, or, for `termination`, whose part before the reported cycle start leads to a marking and whose part after it, not empty, leads from that marking back to it.
The verifier *shall* mark a witness unconfirmed only when the SMT route decided, and *shall* name in each clause part, confirmed or not, a clause of the contract.
The verifier *shall* report a `termination` part only when the contract requires termination, and *shall* name no stranded place in a witness that is not confirmed.
*When* the verdict is `Unknown`, the verifier *shall* give a reason that is not empty.
*If* the closed net declares a match transition, *then* the verifier *shall* return `Proven` or `Violated` only from the SMT route.

**Report order.** Names in a result and its report follow the name order of [VER-013]: the places of every printed marking, the stranded places of the graph route (after the clauses, in contract order), and the stranded places an SMT stranding violation names.

**Cost.** The graph route costs what the closed net's untimed graph costs, which is set by *reachable combinations*, not size. On a node gadget of the shape a compiled workflow produces (`typescript/scripts/bench-open-net.ts`) the class count is 30 from 11 places to 59 and from one outgoing edge to 25, about a millisecond throughout: a node's outgoing edges route together, so correlated edges add places without adding combinations. Edges that route independently multiply instead (30, 42, 66, 114, 210, 402, 1554 classes for one to eight). Across 502 compiled node gadgets the class count is non-monotonic in place count and monotonic in input arity, so an implementation SHOULD report cost to a user in terms of arity rather than size.

The class count also grows with the **concurrent activations** a subnet admits, and with a budget place's tokens only while that number exceeds the budget: an arrival is not budget-gated, starting work is.

- A **join**, whose inputs must all arrive before it fires, runs once whatever the budget and is budget-blind (30 classes at arity two and 42 at arity three, identical at budgets one, two, four and eight; 464 of 464 join gadgets in the corpus). It still grows combinatorially in arity: 30, 42, 66 and 210 classes for arities two, three, four and six.
- An **OR**, several producer edges feeding one input, activates once per arrival *that starts work* (an arrival routed to a skip path spends no budget), so the budget binds while two or more activations can be in flight: a three-arrival OR whose producers can all deliver data has 402, 516, 546, 546, 546 classes for budgets one to eight, the same subnet with one data producer 228 at every budget. No gadget of the 502 changes between budgets 4 and 8. Which real OR gadgets are budget-sensitive is open: over 31 of them neither producer exclusivity nor a loop-back edge predicts it.

An implementation SHOULD describe the claim as blind to the budget above the subnet's concurrent-activation count, not as unconditional budget-independence. An internal 1-safe mutex serialising activations adds a 6–13% constant to the class count and does not move that point.

The SMT route costs two to four hundred times as much on the same subnets (193–418 ms from one edge to eight) and, unlike the graph, grows with size: it is the fallback for a graph that does not close, not an alternative to one.

notes.text:
- TypeScript: `verification/open-net`: `verifyOpenNet(net, contract, options)`; `OpenNetContract.builder()` (`initialMarking`, `arrive`, `arriveAtMost`, `arriveBetween`, `expect`, `expectBetween`, `rest`, `terminal`, `environment`, `requireTermination`); `closeOpenNet`; `StateClassGraph.build(…, { untimed: true })`; `rest-set` `strandedPlaces`.
- Rust: behind the `z3` feature, `open_net`: `verify_open_net(&net, &contract, &options)` with `OpenNetOptions::default()` and its `with_*` setters (`with_max_classes`, `with_smt`, `with_configure_smt`, `with_termination_timeout_ms`, `with_cancel`, `with_assume_no_reaping`, `with_assume_atomic_firing`; the struct is `#[non_exhaustive]`); `OpenNetContract::builder()` (the TypeScript methods in snake case, plus `initial_tokens`; `expect_between` takes `max: Option<usize>`); `close_open_net`; `StateClassGraph::build_with_options(…, StateClassGraphOptions { untimed: true })`; `rest_set::stranded_places`.
- Python: `verify_open_net(net, contract, *, max_classes=50_000, smt=True, termination_timeout_ms=60_000, ...)`; the remaining keywords (`timeout_ms`, `linear_bound`, `state_equation`, `state_equation_phase`, `firing_bound`, `semiflow_invariants`, `cancel`, `assume_no_reaping`, `assume_atomic_firing`, `mint_transitions`) configure each SMT query as for `verify`. `OpenNetContract.builder()` as in Rust, places as varargs, unbounded `max` as `math.inf`. Results: `OpenNetResult`, `ContractViolation`, `PortStep`.
- Java: `org.libpetri.smt.opennet`: `OpenNetVerifier.verifyOpenNet(net, contract, options)` with `OpenNetOptions(maxClasses, smt, configureSmt, terminationTimeout, assumeNoReaping, assumeAtomicFiring)` (the four- and five-argument constructors remain, and `OpenNetOptions.DEFAULT.with...()` changes one option); `OpenNetContract.builder()` (the TypeScript methods plus `initialTokens`; `expectBetween` takes an `OptionalInt` `max`); `OpenNetClosure.closeOpenNet`; `StateClassGraph.build(…, StateClassGraph.Options.UNTIMED)`; `RestSet.strandedPlaces`. Results: `OpenNetResult`, `ContractViolation`, `ContractViolation.PortStep`. Contract places are matched to the net's by name, although Java `Place` equality also compares the token type.
- Every implementation's report is byte-identical to TypeScript's.

     every terminal marker as a waiver;

     firings. Without a ranking termination is undecided, and the report names the firings the

above 0, every reachable quiescent marking meets the contract and, where termination is required, no

*shall* name no stranded place in a witness that is not confirmed.

*If* the closed net declares a match transition, *then* the verifier *shall* return `Proven` or
`Violated` only from the SMT route.

**Report order.** Names in a result and its report follow the name order of [VER-013]: the places
of every printed marking, the stranded places of the graph route (after the clauses, in contract
order), and the stranded places an SMT stranding violation names.

**Acceptance Criteria:**
1. A subnet that meets its contract is `Proven`. The same subnet with an edge that receives
   neither of its two places is `Violated`: the violation names that edge's clause and
   carries a port trace ending in the quiescent marking.
2. A clause whose upper bound is exceeded is violated whether or not a terminal is marked. A
   lower bound is waived while one is.
3. A token on a place the contract does not name is reported as stranded, and the report
   names the place whenever its witness is confirmed, always on the graph route.
4. A reachable cycle is a `termination` violation with a lasso witness when termination is
   required, and no violation when it is waived.
5. An arrival group that must deliver `n` tokens reaches quiescence only after all `n`; a
   group that may deliver at most `n` also reaches quiescence after fewer.
6. A timed subnet gets the verdict of the untimed, reap-aware claim of [VER-004]: its class
   count equals that of the same subnet with every transition immediate, and its verdict equals
   that subnet's when no transition is reapable or under `assumeNoReaping`. On the SMT route, a
   ν-net whose timing keeps a transition from firing is judged as if it could: a stranding only
   that transition causes is `Violated`.
7. When the graph does not close, the SMT route decides. The result is `Unknown`, naming
   the reason, when that route is disabled or leaves a part undecided.
8. An environment transition's firings are marked as environment steps in the port trace. A
   token left on an environment place is never reported stranded; a place environment
   transitions share with the subnet is judged like any other.
9. A closed net with match transitions is not decided by the graph. On two independently
   minted names reaching a join that requires them equal, the join can never fire and both
   inputs strand: the result is `Violated` on the SMT route, never `Proven` by enumeration, and
   `Unknown` naming the skipped graph when the SMT route is disabled.
10. A subnet that strands places whose locale, UTF-16 code-unit and code-point orders differ
    (`Zeit`, `apfel`, U+E000, U+1F600) lists them in code-point order ([VER-013]), in its
    violations on either route and in the quiescent marking its report prints.
11. The relay `q → relay → out` with `relay` at `window(3, 5)`, one arrival on `q` and the
    clause `out = exactly 1`, is `Violated` on the graph route and on the SMT route: a late
    executor reaps the relay and rests with the token on `q`. With `assumeNoReaping` it is
    `Proven` on both, and the report says the verdict assumes no transition is reaped.

**Cost.** The graph route costs what the closed net's untimed graph costs, which is set by
*reachable combinations*, not size. On a node gadget of the shape a compiled workflow produces
(`typescript/scripts/bench-open-net.ts`) the class count is 30 from 11 places to 59 and from one
outgoing edge to 25, about a millisecond throughout: a node's outgoing edges route together, so
correlated edges add places without adding combinations. Edges that route independently multiply
instead (30, 42, 66, 114, 210, 402, 1554 classes for one to eight). Across 502 compiled node
gadgets the class count is non-monotonic in place count and monotonic in input arity, so an
implementation SHOULD report cost to a user in terms of arity rather than size.

The class count also grows with the **concurrent activations** a subnet admits, and with a budget
place's tokens only while that number exceeds the budget: an arrival is not budget-gated, starting
work is.
- A **join**, whose inputs must all arrive before it fires, runs once whatever the budget and is
  budget-blind (30 classes at arity two and 42 at arity three, identical at budgets one, two, four
  and eight; 464 of 464 join gadgets in the corpus). It still grows combinatorially in arity: 30,
  42, 66 and 210 classes for arities two, three, four and six.
- An **OR**, several producer edges feeding one input, activates once per arrival *that starts
  work* (an arrival routed to a skip path spends no budget), so the budget binds while two or more
  activations can be in flight: a three-arrival OR whose producers can all deliver data has 402,
  516, 546, 546, 546 classes for budgets one to eight, the same subnet with one data producer 228
  at every budget. No gadget of the 502 changes between budgets 4 and 8. Which real OR gadgets are
  budget-sensitive is open: over 31 of them neither producer exclusivity nor a loop-back edge
  predicts it.

An implementation SHOULD describe the claim as blind to the budget above the subnet's
concurrent-activation count, not as unconditional budget-independence. An internal 1-safe mutex
serialising activations adds a 6–13% constant to the class count and does not move that point.

The SMT route costs two to four hundred times as much on the same subnets (193–418 ms from one
edge to eight) and, unlike the graph, grows with size: it is the fallback for a graph that does not
close, not an alternative to one.

**Implementation notes:**
- TypeScript: `verification/open-net`: `verifyOpenNet(net, contract, options)`;
  `OpenNetContract.builder()` (`initialMarking`, `arrive`, `arriveAtMost`, `arriveBetween`,
  `expect`, `expectBetween`, `rest`, `terminal`, `environment`, `requireTermination`);
  `closeOpenNet`; `StateClassGraph.build(…, { untimed: true })`; `rest-set` `strandedPlaces`.
- Rust: behind the `z3` feature, `open_net`: `verify_open_net(&net, &contract, &options)` with
  `OpenNetOptions::default()` and its `with_*` setters (`with_max_classes`, `with_smt`,
  `with_configure_smt`, `with_termination_timeout_ms`, `with_cancel`, `with_assume_no_reaping`,
  `with_assume_atomic_firing`; the struct is `#[non_exhaustive]`);
  `OpenNetContract::builder()` (the TypeScript methods in snake case, plus `initial_tokens`;
  `expect_between` takes `max: Option<usize>`); `close_open_net`;
  `StateClassGraph::build_with_options(…, StateClassGraphOptions { untimed: true })`;
  `rest_set::stranded_places`.
- Python: `verify_open_net(net, contract, *, max_classes=50_000, smt=True,
  termination_timeout_ms=60_000, ...)`; the remaining keywords (`timeout_ms`, `linear_bound`,
  `state_equation`, `state_equation_phase`, `firing_bound`, `semiflow_invariants`, `cancel`,
  `assume_no_reaping`, `assume_atomic_firing`, `mint_transitions`) configure each SMT query as
  for `verify`. `OpenNetContract.builder()` as in Rust, places as varargs, unbounded
  `max` as `math.inf`. Results: `OpenNetResult`, `ContractViolation`, `PortStep`.
- Java: `org.libpetri.smt.opennet`: `OpenNetVerifier.verifyOpenNet(net, contract, options)` with
  `OpenNetOptions(maxClasses, smt, configureSmt, terminationTimeout, assumeNoReaping,
  assumeAtomicFiring)` (the four- and five-argument constructors remain, and
  `OpenNetOptions.DEFAULT.with...()` changes one option); `OpenNetContract.builder()`
  (the TypeScript methods plus `initialTokens`; `expectBetween` takes an `OptionalInt` `max`);
  `OpenNetClosure.closeOpenNet`;
  `StateClassGraph.build(…, StateClassGraph.Options.UNTIMED)`; `RestSet.strandedPlaces`. Results:
  `OpenNetResult`, `ContractViolation`, `ContractViolation.PortStep`. Contract places are matched
  to the net's by name, although Java `Place` equality also compares the token type.
- Every implementation's report is byte-identical to TypeScript's.

**Depends on:** [VER-002], [VER-003], [VER-004], [VER-006], [VER-010], [VER-012], [VER-013],
[VER-014], [VER-017], [VER-019], [TIME-013], [EXEC-042], [CORE-043], [NU-010]

**Test derivation:** Use a node gadget: one input edge carrying data or empty, one output with
two edges, a shared budget, and a halt that inhibits start and skip. Its contract is proven.
Then check that each defect breaks the named part:
- a skip that writes only the first edge's empty violates the second edge's clause;
- a run that writes both data and empty on one edge violates that clause's upper bound;
- a done that keeps the budget violates the budget clause;
- a transition that re-marks its own input is a termination violation;
- without the terminal, a halt strands the arrival.

For environment transitions, use a node that sends a request and runs again on each answer.
Its environment answers at most twice, from a budget of its own, or ends the exchange. The
contract is proven with termination required, the budget the environment leaves unspent is
not stranded, and the environment's firings are marked in the port trace.
acceptance: A subnet that meets its contract is `Proven`. The same subnet with an edge that receives neither of its two places is `Violated`: the violation names that edge's clause and carries a port trace ending in the quiescent marking.
A clause whose upper bound is exceeded is violated whether or not a terminal is marked. A lower bound is waived while one is.
A token on a place the contract does not name is reported as stranded, and the report names the place whenever its witness is confirmed, always on the graph route.
A reachable cycle is a `termination` violation with a lasso witness when termination is required, and no violation when it is waived.
An arrival group that must deliver `n` tokens reaches quiescence only after all `n`; a group that may deliver at most `n` also reaches quiescence after fewer.

A timed subnet gets the verdict of the untimed, reap-aware claim of [VER-004]: its class count equals that of the same subnet with every transition immediate, and its verdict equals that subnet's when no transition is reapable or under `assumeNoReaping`. On the SMT route, a ν-net whose timing keeps a transition from firing is judged as if it could: a stranding only that transition causes is `Violated`.
When the graph does not close, the SMT route decides. The result is `Unknown`, naming the reason, when that route is disabled or leaves a part undecided.

An environment transition's firings are marked as environment steps in the port trace. A token left on an environment place is never reported stranded; a place environment transitions share with the subnet is judged like any other.

A closed net with match transitions is not decided by the graph. On two independently minted names reaching a join that requires them equal, the join can never fire and both inputs strand: the result is `Violated` on the SMT route, never `Proven` by enumeration, and `Unknown` naming the skipped graph when the SMT route is disabled.

A subnet that strands places whose locale, UTF-16 code-unit and code-point orders differ (`Zeit`, `apfel`, U+E000, U+1F600) lists them in code-point order ([VER-013]), in its violations on either route and in the quiescent marking its report prints.

The relay `q → relay → out` with `relay` at `window(3, 5)`, one arrival on `q` and the clause `out = exactly 1`, is `Violated` on the graph route and on the SMT route: a late executor reaps the relay and rests with the token on `q`. With `assumeNoReaping` it is `Proven` on both, and the report says the verdict assumes no transition is reaped.

requirements.title: ExecutionCompleted Event
requirements.testDerivation: Run a net to quiescence; verify the last event is ExecutionCompleted, emitted once; with a firing clock that advances during the run, verify the duration is at least the time between the run's ExecutionStarted and ExecutionCompleted.

spans.text: *When* the executor finishes a run ([EXEC-041]), it *shall* emit exactly one ExecutionCompleted event, whatever the termination reason.
spans.label: s1

spans.text: The executor *shall* emit ExecutionCompleted events only when it finishes a run.
spans.label: s2

spans.text: *If* the executor has emitted the ExecutionCompleted event of a run, *then* it *shall not* emit another event of that run other than a log message ([EVT-013]) or an ActionTimedOut event ([EVT-010]).
spans.label: s3

spans.text: *When* the executor finishes a run with the termination reason `quiescent` ([EXEC-040]), it *shall* have no firing in flight, so every firing of the run has ended before its ExecutionCompleted event.
spans.label: s4

spans.text: *Where* the ExecutionCompleted event carries a total duration (Java and TypeScript), the total duration *shall* be at least the time the run took on the executor's firing clock ([TIME-015]), from the reading at its ExecutionStarted event to the reading at its ExecutionCompleted event.
spans.label: s5

paragraphs.text: Emitted when a run ends: the executor's loop finishes the run, whatever the termination reason ([EXEC-041]). Contains:

- Timestamp
- Net name
- Execution ID (Java and TypeScript, [EVT-002])
- Total duration (Java and TypeScript)
*When* the executor finishes a run ([EXEC-041]), it *shall* emit exactly one ExecutionCompleted event, whatever the termination reason.
The executor *shall* emit ExecutionCompleted events only when it finishes a run.
*If* the executor has emitted the ExecutionCompleted event of a run, *then* it *shall not* emit another event of that run other than a log message ([EVT-013]) or an ActionTimedOut event ([EVT-010]).
*When* the executor finishes a run with the termination reason `quiescent` ([EXEC-040]), it *shall* have no firing in flight, so every firing of the run has ended before its ExecutionCompleted event.

The event marks the end of the run, not its outcome. A run that a terminal stop ([EXEC-042]) or an immediate termination ([ENV-015]) ends can leave firings in flight: both abandon them, and the timer of an abandoned action can still emit its ActionTimedOut after the end. The event carries no termination reason: a consumer reads the reason as [EXEC-041] says, never the event alone as proof that the net quiesced. A loop that a caller's run budget leaves running has not finished, so it emits the event when it finishes, not when the caller's wait ends.

*Where* the ExecutionCompleted event carries a total duration (Java and TypeScript), the total duration *shall* be at least the time the run took on the executor's firing clock ([TIME-015]), from the reading at its ExecutionStarted event to the reading at its ExecutionCompleted event.
Java and TypeScript measure the total duration from the construction of the executor, so for a later run of the same executor it also counts the earlier runs and the time between them.

*When* the executor finishes a run ([EXEC-041]), it *shall* emit exactly one ExecutionCompleted event, whatever the termination reason.

*If* the executor has emitted the ExecutionCompleted event of a run, *then* it *shall not* emit another event of that run other than a log message ([EVT-013]) or an ActionTimedOut event ([EVT-010]).

*When* the executor finishes a run with the termination reason `quiescent` ([EXEC-040]), it *shall* have no firing in flight, so every firing of the run has ended before its ExecutionCompleted event.

1. Emitted exactly once per run that finishes, whatever the termination reason, and followed by no event of the run other than a log message or an ActionTimedOut.

paragraphs.text: Emitted when a transition action produces log output. The engine captures log statements from within actions and wraps them as events. Contains:

- Timestamp
- Transition name, empty or absent when no transition is responsible for the message (see below)
- Logger name (Java and TypeScript)
- Log level
- Message
- Error/throwable details (optional; Java and TypeScript)

*Where* the implementation captures the log statements of actions (Java and TypeScript), the executor *shall* report each log statement it captures from the action of a firing as one LogMessage event that carries the firing's transition name, the statement's level and its message.

**The engine may also emit diagnostics of its own** through this event rather than adding an event type per diagnostic: a dead arc ([CORE-037]), an unknown place ([CORE-072]), a repeated output place ([IO-016]), and similar. A diagnostic that a transition is responsible for carries that transition's name: the transition that declares the dead arc, or the transition whose firing deposited the tokens. A diagnostic that no transition is responsible for, at the initial-marking and injection seams, carries an empty or absent transition name. Consumers MUST therefore treat the transition name as optional and MUST NOT key, filter or group on it without handling its absence.

*When* the executor emits an engine diagnostic before the first step of a run, the diagnostic *shall* carry an empty or absent transition name, unless it reports a dead arc ([CORE-037]), in which case it *shall* carry the name of the transition that declares the arc.
*When* the executor emits an engine diagnostic as it injects a token into an environment place, the diagnostic *shall* carry an empty or absent transition name.

*When* the executor emits an engine diagnostic as it deposits the outcome of a firing or a batch that the firing published ([IO-015]), the diagnostic *shall* carry the name of that firing's transition.

An engine diagnostic SHOULD be emitted only where it reports something the caller did not ask for and would otherwise not learn. A diagnostic on a path the caller explicitly requested, such as a `close()` it called itself ([ENV-013]), is a false positive: it fires on every run of a net whose normal ending is a shutdown ([ENV-012]), and a warning that always fires trains its reader to ignore the level. Where a queryable result already carries the information ([EXEC-041] AC3), the event is an addition to it and MUST NOT be the only signal.

*When* the caller drains, closes or stops the executor ([ENV-011], [ENV-013], [ENV-015]), the executor *shall not* emit an engine diagnostic for the request or for the queued external events it discards because of it.
*When* the executor refuses an injection request because it is draining, closed or stopped, or because the run has finished ([ENV-006]), it *shall not* emit an engine diagnostic for the refusal.
*When* a run ends because it is quiescent, a terminal place is marked, or the caller closed or stopped it ([EXEC-041]), the executor *shall not* emit an engine diagnostic for that end.

- Java: Captures SLF4J output via LogCaptureScope
- TypeScript: Captures via context.log() method
- Rust: Emits the engine diagnostics as LogMessage events, but does not capture the log statements of actions (the transition context's log function is never installed); Python, which runs on Rust, captures none either.

*When* the executor emits an engine diagnostic before the first step of a run, the diagnostic *shall* carry an empty or absent transition name, unless it reports a dead arc ([CORE-037]), in which case it *shall* carry the name of the transition that declares the arc.

*When* the executor emits an engine diagnostic as it injects a token into an environment place, the diagnostic *shall* carry an empty or absent transition name.

*When* the executor emits an engine diagnostic as it deposits the outcome of a firing or a batch that the firing published ([IO-015]), the diagnostic *shall* carry the name of that firing's transition.

An engine diagnostic SHOULD be emitted only where it reports something the caller did not ask for
and would otherwise not learn. A diagnostic on a path the caller explicitly requested, such as a
`close()` it called itself ([ENV-013]), is a false positive: it fires on every run of a net whose
normal ending is a shutdown ([ENV-012]), and a warning that always fires trains its reader to
ignore the level. Where a queryable result already carries the information ([EXEC-041] AC3), the
event is an addition to it and MUST NOT be the only signal.

*When* the caller drains, closes or stops the executor ([ENV-011], [ENV-013], [ENV-015]), the executor *shall not* emit an engine diagnostic for the request or for the queued external events it discards because of it.

*When* the executor refuses an injection request because it is draining, closed or stopped, or because the run has finished ([ENV-006]), it *shall not* emit an engine diagnostic for the refusal.

*When* a run ends because it is quiescent, a terminal place is marked, or the caller closed or stopped it ([EXEC-041]), the executor *shall not* emit an engine diagnostic for that end.

**Acceptance Criteria:**
1. Log statements within actions are captured as LogMessage events.
2. Log level (INFO, WARN, ERROR, etc.) is preserved.
3. Exception details are included when present.
4. An engine diagnostic that no transition is responsible for carries an empty or absent
   transition name, one that a transition is responsible for carries that transition's name, and
   every consumer of the event tolerates an absent name.
5. No engine diagnostic is emitted on a caller-requested termination path (a drain, a close or a
   stop), nor when a run ends as quiescent, terminal, closed or stopped, nor when an injection
   request is refused.

**Depends on:** [CORE-072], [ENV-012], [ENV-013], [EXEC-041]
**Implementation notes:**
- Java: Captures SLF4J output via LogCaptureScope
- TypeScript: Captures via context.log() method
- Rust: Emits the engine diagnostics as LogMessage events, but does not capture the log statements of actions (the transition context's log function is never installed); Python, which runs on Rust, captures none either.

**Test derivation:** Action logs a warning; verify LogMessage event with correct level and message.

An engine diagnostic that no transition is responsible for carries an empty or absent transition name, one that a transition is responsible for carries that transition's name, and every consumer of the event tolerates an absent name.

No engine diagnostic is emitted on a caller-requested termination path (a drain, a close or a stop), nor when a run ends as quiescent, terminal, closed or stopped, nor when an injection request is refused.

- Timestamp

*When* a run finishes ([EXEC-041]), whatever its termination reason, the executor *shall* emit a MarkingSnapshot event that carries the marking the run ends with and, after it, an ExecutionCompleted event.

The marking a MarkingSnapshot event carries *shall* list every place the net declares that holds a token, *shall* list each place it lists with all of that place's tokens in FIFO order, and *shall not* list a place that holds no token.

The marking a MarkingSnapshot event carries *shall* list each place at most once and *shall* list its places in ascending code-point order of the place name, also for a place name above U+FFFF ([CORE-073]).
A place the net does not declare may be listed with its tokens or left out.

A marking snapshot carried on this event is the snapshot form of [CORE-073], and [CORE-073]'s canonical place-order rule applies to it: the places of the marking it carries MUST appear in ascending code-point order of the place name. The event is an ordered, in-process value, so the order is both meetable and observable there, and it is one of the two places a host takes a snapshot from.

The order is **not** promised past the event. A JSON session archive ([EVT-025]) and the JSON debug protocol are unordered media, and code-point order is deliberately not required of them. What is required of any rendering of this event — those two included — is **reproducibility across runs of the same implementation**: two runs over identical data MUST produce identical output, so a rendering MUST NOT pass the marking through a container whose iteration order is randomised per process ([CORE-073]).
Emitting this event MUST NOT fail the run. In particular the refusal [CORE-073] requires for two same-named places belongs to the host-facing snapshot and restore operations, not to this event.

*When* an event is appended to the logging event store, the store *shall* log the event once, at the level of the event's kind, *shall* then pass the event once to the wrapped store, and *shall* log no other record and pass no other event, whatever store it wraps.

The logging event store *shall* log TransitionFailed, TransitionTimedOut and ActionTimedOut events at WARN level.

The logging event store *shall* log ExecutionStarted and ExecutionCompleted events at INFO level.

The logging event store *shall* log TransitionEnabled, TransitionClockRestarted, TransitionStarted and TransitionCompleted events at DEBUG level.

The logging event store *shall* report itself as enabled, whatever the wrapped store reports (`isEnabled()` returns true).

2. Lifecycle events (ExecutionStarted, ExecutionCompleted) logged at INFO level.
3. The other transition events (TransitionEnabled, TransitionClockRestarted, TransitionStarted, TransitionCompleted) logged at DEBUG level.
4. Token events (TokenAdded, TokenRemoved), MarkingSnapshot and LogMessage logged at TRACE level.

requirements.body:
An event store with live tailing support for debug UIs. Supports:
- Subscriptions (consumers notified of new events)
- Capacity management (eviction of old events)
- Session tracking

A debug event store has a capacity: a positive number of events, 10,000 unless the caller gives another. A debug event store is open until its `close()` is called.

*When* events have been appended to a debug event store one after the other, a call of `events()` *shall* return the newest of them, as many as the store's capacity allows, in the order they were appended.

*When* an event is appended to an open debug event store, the append *shall* complete without waiting for any subscriber to receive the event.

Each subscriber of a debug event store *shall* receive only events appended to the store, each at most once and, for appends that do not overlap in time, in the order they were appended. A subscriber may receive an event after the append that added it has returned.

*While* a debug event store is open, a caller *shall* be able to add a further subscriber, whatever subscribers the store already has.

*While* a debug event store is open, each subscriber that has not cancelled its subscription *shall* still be able to receive every event appended since it subscribed, whatever the other subscribers have received.

**Acceptance Criteria:**
1. While the store is open, each subscriber that has not cancelled can receive the events appended since it subscribed, each at most once and, for appends that do not overlap in time, in the order they were appended.
2. Old events are evicted when capacity is exceeded.
3. Multiple subscribers can be active simultaneously.

**Implementation notes:**

- TypeScript: Full implementation with microtask broadcast
- Rust: Implemented (`libpetri-debug::DebugEventStore`, crossbeam-channel subscriptions)

paragraphs.text: Completed debug sessions can be serialized to a length-prefixed compressed archive (LZ4 for Java, gzip for TypeScript and Rust) for later replay. The archive has a versioned header followed by one length-prefixed JSON record per event.
Three header versions exist; readers MUST accept all three and dispatch into the matching sealed variant (`V1`/`V2`/`V3`) so callers can pattern-match on writer guarantees.
**Header format** (the same field names and JSON types in every language; the encoding of time values differs, see below):

| Header | First shipped | Adds over previous |
|---|---|---|
| v1 | libpetri 1.5.x | baseline: `sessionId`, `netName`, `dotDiagram`, `startTime`, `eventCount`, `structure` |
| v2 | libpetri 1.7.x | `endTime`, `tags`, pre-computed `metadata` (event-type histogram, first/last, hasErrors) |
| v3 | libpetri 1.8.0 | same fields as v2; bump signals typed-token event bodies |

**Event body format** (per-language, because each implementation serializes its own event shape — Java serializes the `NetEvent` record directly, TypeScript and Rust serialize a `NetEventInfo` debug-protocol projection). Archive bodies are therefore not byte-compatible across languages, and neither are whole archives: Java compresses with LZ4 and the others with gzip, and every time value (the header's `startTime` and `endTime`, the event and token timestamps of the body) is ISO-8601 text in Java and TypeScript and decimal epoch milliseconds in Rust and Python. The Rust reader rejects an archive whose event timestamps are ISO-8601 text, and the TypeScript reader reads decimal epoch milliseconds as invalid dates, so an archive is read correctly only by an implementation of the language that wrote it. All languages agree on *semantic* content, not wire layout.

- **Java (v3):** `token: {valueType: <FQN>, v: <structured JSON>, createdAt: <iso>}`. Special cases: `{valueType: "void", createdAt}` for unit tokens (no `v`); `{valueType, text, createdAt}` fallback when Jackson cannot structure the value; legacy `{value, valueType: simpleName, createdAt}` from v1/v2 also accepted.
- **TypeScript (v3):** `token: {id, type, value: <String(value)>, structured?: <JSON>, timestamp}`. The `value` string is retained alongside the new optional `structured` field so the bundled debug UI keeps rendering without change. `type` is `value.constructor.name` (simple name — TypeScript has no portable FQN).
- **Rust (v3):** `token: {id, type, value, structured?, timestamp}`, with the field names and JSON shapes of TypeScript via a shared `NetEventInfo` camelCase serde contract; the `timestamp` is decimal epoch milliseconds where TypeScript writes ISO-8601 text. `type` is `std::any::type_name::<T>()` at token-erasure time; `structured` is populated by [`TokenProjectorRegistry`](../rust/libpetri-debug/src/token_projector_registry.rs) when the token's inner `T` is registered, else falls back to `{"type": <type_name>, "text": <Debug repr>}` — parallel to Java's `{valueType, text}` shape.

**Key order in an archive is not guaranteed, and [CORE-073]'s canonical order does not reach it.** A JSON object is an *unordered* collection by definition, so an archive that renders a marking as one carries no order regardless of what the producer did. Some implementations preserve insertion order incidentally; JavaScript cannot, because it orders integer-like keys numerically ahead of every other key whatever the insertion order — a net with a place named `2` reorders itself. The JSON debug protocol is the same medium and is bound the same way.

This is a bound on the medium, not a defect to fix: canonical order is guaranteed **on the snapshot form and on the event** ([CORE-073], [EVT-014]), which is where a host that hashes, diffs or content-addresses should take it. A host needing a byte-stable archive artefact *across implementations* MUST canonicalise at its own serialization boundary rather than relying on the object's key order.

What the medium does not excuse is **irreproducibility**. An archive written twice by the same implementation from identical run data MUST NOT differ ([CORE-073], [EVT-014] AC5). JavaScript's numeric-first key order is arbitrary but fixed, so it satisfies this; a marking copied through a per-process-randomised map does not, and an implementation MUST NOT put one on the path to the archive or the debug protocol. This asks for no change of archive format.

*Where* an implementation provides session archives, *when* its reader reads a well-formed archive of header version 1, 2 or 3 in its own implementation's format (one whose `eventCount` and metadata are those of its body, as its writer writes them), the reader *shall* return the header variant of that version (`V1`, `V2` or `V3`).

*Where* an implementation provides session archives, *if* its reader reads an archive in its own implementation's format whose header version is not 1, 2 or 3, *then* the reader *shall* reject the archive with the error `Unsupported archive version: <version> (reader supports 1..3)`, which names the version it found and the supported range.

*Where* an implementation provides session archives, *when* its reader accepts a well-formed archive in its own implementation's format, it *shall* return the header's `eventCount` unchanged, the header's session fields and metadata as written, and one event for each record of the body, in body order.

*Where* an implementation provides session archives, *when* its writer writes an archive of a session for header version 1, 2 or 3 (`writeV1`, `writeV2`, or `write` for version 3), the header *shall* carry that version and the session's own header fields.

*Where* an implementation provides session archives, *when* its writer writes an archive, the writer *shall* take one snapshot of the event store, the header's `eventCount` *shall* be the number of events in that snapshot, a V1 header *shall* carry no metadata, the V2 and V3 metadata *shall* be computed from that snapshot, and the body *shall* hold one record for each event of that snapshot, in the order of the snapshot.
*Where* an implementation provides session archives, two archives its writer writes for the same header version from identical run data *shall* be identical.

*Where* an implementation provides session archives, its writer *shall* write an archive of any session for each of the header versions 1, 2 and 3 (`writeV1`, `writeV2`, and `write` for version 3), whatever the session's event store holds.

notes.text:
- Java: Full implementation — default writer emits v3, deserializer reconstructs original token types via `Class.forName`. The V2 and V3 header holds the tags and the metadata histogram in ascending code-point order of their keys, so two JVMs write the same header for the same run data.
- TypeScript: Full implementation — default writer emits v3, `structured` projection via `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(value))`.
- Rust: Full implementation — default writer emits v3 via a user-supplied `TokenProjectorRegistry`; reader hydrates into a `ReplayedTokenPayload` exposing the `structured` JSON without attempting to revive the original `T` (Rust has no `Class.forName` equivalent).
- Python: `SessionArchiveWriter.write_from_store` writes version 3 through the Rust writer, and `write_v1` and `write_v2` write versions 1 and 2. Each archives every event of the store's snapshot, whatever its size, and a header whose `structure` lists the net's places and transitions. For an empty store the start time is 0 and there is no end time, so two archives of the same empty session are identical.
notes.label: Implementation notes

notes.text: Java → Java reconstructs typed tokens. TypeScript and Rust archive bodies share field names and JSON shapes (shared `NetEventInfo` contract) but not the time encoding, so neither reader reads the other's archives correctly; both preserve `structured` across a round-trip. Java archive bodies use a different shape (`NetEvent` direct serialization) and are not interchangeable at the body level — use language-native archives for full-fidelity replay.
notes.label: Cross-language replay

notes.text: Java v3 deserialization resolves the archive-supplied `valueType` FQN via `Class.forName`. TypeScript's `structuredValue` uses `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(v))` — safe against code execution and prototype pollution, but respects any `toJSON()` method on the value. Rust's `TokenProjectorRegistry` projects only user-registered types; unregistered values fall back to `Debug` repr and never execute arbitrary code. Archives are a trust boundary: **do not deserialize archives from untrusted network sources** without a guard — in Java because of static-initializer side effects, in TypeScript because a hostile `toJSON()` override could return misleading data, and in Rust because a hostile archive could claim any `type_name` string.

paragraphs.text: The event store or helper functions support:

- Filter by event type
- Filter by transition name
- Filter by place name (for token events)
- Pagination (offset / limit) over the filtered result
- Filter for failure events
- Count events, and an event-type histogram (counters)

*Where* an implementation provides a query over the events of an event store, the query without offset and limit *shall* return exactly the events that `events()` returns and that match every filter the query gives, in the order `events()` returns them, for every query whose transition filter does not name the empty name.

A filter by event type *shall* match the events of the given types, a filter by transition name *shall* match the events that carry one of the given transition names, and a filter by place name *shall* match the events that carry one of the given place names.
An event that carries no transition name *shall* match no filter by transition name, and its presence in the store *shall not* change which other events such a filter returns.

*Where* an implementation provides offset and limit on a query, the query *shall* skip the first `offset` matching events and return the first `limit` of the matching events that follow (all of them when no limit is given), so that the page is taken over the filtered result and not over the store.

*Where* an implementation provides `failures()`, it *shall* return exactly the TransitionFailed, TransitionTimedOut and ActionTimedOut events that `events()` returns, in the order `events()` returns them.

*Where* an implementation provides `counters()`, it *shall* name each event type that occurs among the events `events()` returns exactly once, with the number of those events of that type, and *shall* name no other event type.

requirements.body:
The event store or helper functions support:
- Filter by event type
- Filter by transition name
- Filter by place name (for token events)
- Pagination (offset / limit) over the filtered result
- Filter for failure events
- Count events, and an event-type histogram (counters)

*Where* an implementation provides a query over the events of an event store, the query without offset and limit *shall* return exactly the events that `events()` returns and that match every filter the query gives, in the order `events()` returns them, for every query whose transition filter does not name the empty name.

A filter by event type *shall* match the events of the given types, a filter by transition name *shall* match the events that carry one of the given transition names, and a filter by place name *shall* match the events that carry one of the given place names.

An event that carries no transition name *shall* match no filter by transition name, and its presence in the store *shall not* change which other events such a filter returns.

*Where* an implementation provides offset and limit on a query, the query *shall* skip the first `offset` matching events and return the first `limit` of the matching events that follow (all of them when no limit is given), so that the page is taken over the filtered result and not over the store.

*Where* an implementation provides `failures()`, it *shall* return exactly the TransitionFailed, TransitionTimedOut and ActionTimedOut events that `events()` returns, in the order `events()` returns them.

*Where* an implementation provides `counters()`, it *shall* name each event type that occurs among the events `events()` returns exactly once, with the number of those events of that type, and *shall* name no other event type.

*Where* an implementation provides a count of events, the count *shall* be the number of events that `events()` returns whose type is one of the given types, or the number of all of them when no type is given.

**Acceptance Criteria:**
1. `eventsOfType(TransitionCompleted)` returns only completed events.
2. `transitionEvents("MyTransition")` returns all events that carry that transition name, also when the store holds events that carry no transition name.
3. Place filtering returns only token events for the named place(s); offset/limit page the result.
4. `failures()` returns TransitionFailed, TransitionTimedOut, and ActionTimedOut events.
5. `counters()` returns a `{eventType: count}` histogram whose values sum to the total event count.

**Test derivation:** Run net with mixed events; verify each filter, pagination, and the counters
histogram return correct subsets / totals.

`failures()` returns TransitionFailed, TransitionTimedOut, and ActionTimedOut events.
`counters()` returns a `{eventType: count}` histogram whose values sum to the total event count.

requirements.body:
An event store may expose a live subscription that streams events as they are appended, distinct
from the post-hoc snapshot reads of [EVT-020]. A subscription:
- delivers only events matching its server-side filters (by type, transition, and place);
- is forward-only: events appended **before** the subscription was created are not replayed;
- batches delivery by a caller-chosen `batch_size` and `batch_timeout_ms` (a `batch_size = 1`,
  `batch_timeout_ms = 0` "unary" mode delivers one event at a time for low latency);
- is bounded: it uses a finite channel capacity, and an append of a matching event that finds the channel full ends that subscription instead of waiting for room;
- terminates cleanly on explicit close, when the store is dropped, or when its channel overflows.

This differs from [EVT-024] (DebugEventStore live tailing for debug UIs): EVT-031 governs
subscriptions over the ordinary observability store, with server-side filtering and batching.

*Where* an event store provides live subscriptions, the events a subscription has received at any point, taken over all its batches in the order it received them, *shall* be events that match its filters and were appended to the store after the subscription was created and before that point, in append order, each at most once.

Each batch a subscription receives *shall* hold at least one event and at most `batch_size` events, so that with `batch_size = 1` it receives one event per batch.

Each subscription *shall* have a finite channel capacity.

*When* a receive has taken the first event of its batch, it *shall* add further events until the batch holds `batch_size` events, `batch_timeout_ms` have elapsed since it took that first event, or no further event can arrive, and *shall* then return the batch; with `batch_timeout_ms = 0` it *shall* add only the events already in the channel.

*When* an append of an event that matches the filters of a subscription finds its channel full, the store *shall* end that subscription: the subscription *shall* receive no event appended from then on, and, if none of its receives is pending at that append, its receives *shall* take the events its channel holds and then report the end of the stream, unless the subscription is closed first.

Until the store is dropped, an append *shall* be accepted at every point; in particular it *shall not* wait for room in the channel of a subscription.

*When* a subscription is closed while none of its receives is pending, it *shall* receive no further event, and its next receive *shall* report the end of the stream.

*When* the store is dropped, the receives of each of its subscriptions that has no receive pending *shall* take the events its channel holds and then report the end of the stream, unless the subscription is closed first.

What a close or an overflow does to a receive that is already pending is not specified.

**Acceptance Criteria:**
1. A subscriber receives only events matching its filters, in append order.
2. Events appended before the subscription are not delivered (forward-only).
3. Unary mode delivers one event per batch; batched mode delivers up to `batch_size`, flushing
   early after `batch_timeout_ms`.
4. Explicit close with no receive pending ends iteration cleanly; a full channel ends the subscription: it receives no later event, the append does not wait, and with no receive pending its receives report the end after they have taken the events its channel holds.

**Depends on:** [EVT-020], [EVT-021], [EVT-030]
**Status:** Proposed
**Test derivation:** Run an async net feeding environment events; subscribe with a transition
filter; verify batched forward-only delivery and clean close.
acceptance: A subscriber receives only events matching its filters, in append order.

requirements.title: Marking Replay Cache
requirements.testDerivation: Record a multi-firing run; `compute_at` at 0, an intermediate index, the end, and beyond-end; verify clamping and snapshot reuse. Run a net with token 1 in place 0 and one transition that takes it and puts 9 back; before the first step and after each step, compare the replayed counts with the executor's marking and check that every transition that holds a clock is listed as enabled.

spans.text: *While* every snapshot in the replay cache is at an index no greater than the length of `events` and is the replay of `events` up to that index, `compute_at(events, index)` *shall* return the replay of the first `index` events of `events`, or of all of `events` when `index` is beyond its length.
spans.label: s1

spans.text: *When* `compute_at(events, index)` returns, every snapshot it leaves in the replay cache *shall* be at an index no greater than the length of `events` and be the replay of `events` up to that index, provided every snapshot in the cache met both conditions before the call.
spans.label: s2

spans.text: The replay of an event stream *shall* start from the empty state (no token in any place, no enabled and no in-flight transition) and apply its events in order, each as follows: a `MarkingSnapshot` sets the token count of every place it carries to the count it carries and of every other place to zero; a `TokenAdded` adds one token to its place; a `TokenRemoved` removes one token from its place, and does nothing if the place has none; a `TransitionEnabled` adds its transition to the enabled transitions; a `TransitionStarted` removes its transition from the enabled transitions and adds it to the in-flight transitions; a `TransitionCompleted`, `TransitionFailed`, `TransitionTimedOut` or `ActionTimedOut` removes its transition from the in-flight transitions; any other event (`ExecutionStarted`, `ExecutionCompleted`, `TransitionClockRestarted`, `LogMessage`) leaves the state unchanged.
spans.label: s3

spans.text: The replay of all events a run has emitted before its first step, or up to the end of any of its steps, *shall* count, for every place the net declares, the tokens that place holds at that point, and *shall* list among the enabled transitions every transition that holds a clock at that point, also one whose clock restart is pending ([EVT-005]).
spans.label: s4

paragraphs.text: A replay cache reconstructs execution state at an arbitrary event index from a recorded event stream, for debug-protocol seek / step. `compute_at(events, index)` returns a `ComputedState` — the marking (token counts per place), enabled transitions, and in-flight transitions — replayed from the nearest periodically-cached snapshot rather than from the start of the stream.

*While* every snapshot in the replay cache is at an index no greater than the length of `events` and is the replay of `events` up to that index, `compute_at(events, index)` *shall* return the replay of the first `index` events of `events`, or of all of `events` when `index` is beyond its length.

*When* `compute_at(events, index)` returns, every snapshot it leaves in the replay cache *shall* be at an index no greater than the length of `events` and be the replay of `events` up to that index, provided every snapshot in the cache met both conditions before the call.

The replay of an event stream *shall* start from the empty state (no token in any place, no enabled and no in-flight transition) and apply its events in order, each as follows: a `MarkingSnapshot` sets the token count of every place it carries to the count it carries and of every other place to zero; a `TokenAdded` adds one token to its place; a `TokenRemoved` removes one token from its place, and does nothing if the place has none; a `TransitionEnabled` adds its transition to the enabled transitions; a `TransitionStarted` removes its transition from the enabled transitions and adds it to the in-flight transitions; a `TransitionCompleted`, `TransitionFailed`, `TransitionTimedOut` or `ActionTimedOut` removes its transition from the in-flight transitions; any other event (`ExecutionStarted`, `ExecutionCompleted`, `TransitionClockRestarted`, `LogMessage`) leaves the state unchanged.

The enabled transitions are those with a `TransitionEnabled` event and no later `TransitionStarted` event, so they over-approximate the transitions enabled at that point of the run: a transition whose tokens another firing took, or a reaped transition, stays listed. The in-flight transitions are a set of names, so a transition with two firings in flight at once leaves it when its first firing ends. The replayed token counts include the initial marking only for a stream that reports it in a `MarkingSnapshot` right after its `ExecutionStarted` event, as every executor's stream does ([EVT-014]); the replay reads only the counts of a snapshot. The two transition lists of a `ComputedState` are sets: their order is not specified.

The replay of all events a run has emitted before its first step, or up to the end of any of its steps, *shall* count, for every place the net declares, the tokens that place holds at that point, and *shall* list among the enabled transitions every transition that holds a clock at that point, also one whose clock restart is pending ([EVT-005]). At an index inside the events of one step, for example between the `TokenRemoved` events of a firing that starts, the replayed counts can match no marking the executor held. The count is required only on the places the net declares: a TypeScript snapshot lists only the declared places, so the snapshot before `ExecutionCompleted` sets the replayed count of an undeclared place back to zero.

requirements.body:
A replay cache reconstructs execution state at an arbitrary event index from a recorded event
stream, for debug-protocol seek / step. `compute_at(events, index)` returns a `ComputedState`
— the marking (token counts per place), enabled transitions, and in-flight transitions — replayed
from the nearest periodically-cached snapshot rather than from the start of the stream.

*While* every snapshot in the replay cache is at an index no greater than the length of `events` and is the replay of `events` up to that index, `compute_at(events, index)` *shall* return the replay of the first `index` events of `events`, or of all of `events` when `index` is beyond its length.

*When* `compute_at(events, index)` returns, every snapshot it leaves in the replay cache *shall* be at an index no greater than the length of `events` and be the replay of `events` up to that index, provided every snapshot in the cache met both conditions before the call.

The replay of an event stream *shall* start from the empty state (no token in any place, no enabled and no in-flight transition) and apply its events in order, each as follows: a `MarkingSnapshot` sets the token count of every place it carries to the count it carries and of every other place to zero; a `TokenAdded` adds one token to its place; a `TokenRemoved` removes one token from its place, and does nothing if the place has none; a `TransitionEnabled` adds its transition to the enabled transitions; a `TransitionStarted` removes its transition from the enabled transitions and adds it to the in-flight transitions; a `TransitionCompleted`, `TransitionFailed`, `TransitionTimedOut` or `ActionTimedOut` removes its transition from the in-flight transitions; any other event (`ExecutionStarted`, `ExecutionCompleted`, `TransitionClockRestarted`, `LogMessage`) leaves the state unchanged.

The enabled transitions are those with a `TransitionEnabled` event and no later `TransitionStarted` event, so they over-approximate the transitions enabled at that point of the run: a transition whose tokens another firing took, or a reaped transition, stays listed. The in-flight transitions are a set of names, so a transition with two firings in flight at once leaves it when its first firing ends. The replayed token counts include the initial marking only for a stream that reports it in a `MarkingSnapshot` right after its `ExecutionStarted` event, as every executor's stream does ([EVT-014]); the replay reads only the counts of a snapshot. The two transition lists of a `ComputedState` are sets: their order is not specified.

The replay of all events a run has emitted before its first step, or up to the end of any of its steps, *shall* count, for every place the net declares, the tokens that place holds at that point, and *shall* list among the enabled transitions every transition that holds a clock at that point, also one whose clock restart is pending ([EVT-005]). At an index inside the events of one step, for example between the `TokenRemoved` events of a firing that starts, the replayed counts can match no marking the executor held. The count is required only on the places the net declares: a TypeScript snapshot lists only the declared places, so the snapshot before `ExecutionCompleted` sets the replayed count of an undeclared place back to zero.

**Acceptance Criteria:**
1. `compute_at(events, 0)` is the empty state; `compute_at(events, len)` is the replay of the whole
   stream.
2. An index beyond the stream length is clamped to the end (no panic).
3. Repeated calls on a stream that only grows at its end return state equal to a from-scratch
   replay: the same token count per place and the same sets of enabled and in-flight transitions,
   in an unspecified order. A stream that changed otherwise, for example by the eviction of its
   oldest events ([EVT-024]), needs `invalidate()` before the next call. Reusing cached snapshots
   is expected for speed only: it does not change the state returned.
4. The marking in `ComputedState` carries token counts; replayed tokens need not carry value
   payloads (events carry type + structured metadata, not live objects).
5. Before the first step of a run and after each of its steps, the replay of the events emitted
   so far counts on every declared place the tokens it holds, and lists as enabled every
   transition that holds a clock.

**Depends on:** [EVT-021], [EVT-004], [EVT-006], [EVT-007], [EVT-008], [EVT-009], [EVT-010], [EVT-011], [EVT-012], [EVT-014]
**Test derivation:** Record a multi-firing run; `compute_at` at 0, an intermediate index, the end,
and beyond-end; verify clamping and snapshot reuse. Run a net with token 1 in
place 0 and one transition that takes it and puts 9 back; before the first step and after each
step, compare the replayed counts with the executor's marking and check that every transition
that holds a clock is listed as enabled.

An index beyond the stream length is clamped to the end (no panic).

A stream that changed otherwise, for example by the eviction of its oldest events ([EVT-024]), needs `invalidate()` before the next call. Reusing cached snapshots is expected for speed only: it does not change the state returned.
The marking in `ComputedState` carries token counts; replayed tokens need not carry value payloads (events carry type + structured metadata, not live objects).

Before the first step of a run and after each of its steps, the replay of the events emitted so far counts on every declared place the tokens it holds, and lists as enabled every transition that holds a clock.

requirements.testDerivation: Build net with all arc types; export; verify output parses correctly.

spans.text: The engine MUST support exporting the net structure to at least one standard graph format suitable for visualization.
spans.label: s1

spans.text: The export *shall* draw exactly one node for each place on which some transition has an input, output, inhibitor, read or reset arc.
spans.label: s2

spans.text: *Where* the transitions of a net have pairwise distinct names, the export *shall* draw exactly one node for each transition.
spans.label: s3

spans.text: The export *shall* draw a place node only for a place that the net declares or on which some transition has an arc, and a transition node only for a transition of the net.
spans.label: s4

spans.text: The export *shall* draw, for each input arc, inhibitor arc and read arc, an edge of the arc's type from the node of its place to the node of its transition.
spans.label: s5

spans.text: *Where* the transitions of a net have pairwise distinct names, the export *shall* draw as many input, inhibitor and read edges from the node of a place to the node of a transition as the transition has arcs of that type on that place.
spans.label: s6

spans.text: The export *shall* draw into each place that a transition's output spec names an edge from that transition or from one of its junctions, of type output or, where the transition also has a reset arc on that place, of the combined reset+output type of [EXP-013].
spans.label: s7

spans.text: The export *shall* draw into each place on which a transition has a reset arc an edge from that transition or from one of its junctions, of type reset or, where the transition's output spec also names that place, of the combined reset+output type of [EXP-013].
spans.label: s8

requirements.body:
The engine MUST support exporting the net structure to at least one standard graph format suitable for visualization. The canonical format is DOT (Graphviz), a widely-supported, text-based format.

In this chapter the node of a place or a transition is the node that stands for it in the exported graph, whatever its DOT ID ([EXP-014]). A place that the net declares and on which no transition has an arc may have a node or none; a node for it is the intended end state.

The export *shall* draw exactly one node for each place on which some transition has an input, output, inhibitor, read or reset arc.

*Where* the transitions of a net have pairwise distinct names, the export *shall* draw exactly one node for each transition.

The export *shall* draw a place node only for a place that the net declares or on which some transition has an arc, and a transition node only for a transition of the net.

The export *shall* draw, for each input arc, inhibitor arc and read arc, an edge of the arc's type from the node of its place to the node of its transition.

*Where* the transitions of a net have pairwise distinct names, the export *shall* draw as many input, inhibitor and read edges from the node of a place to the node of a transition as the transition has arcs of that type on that place.

The export *shall* draw into each place that a transition's output spec names an edge from that transition or from one of its junctions, of type output or, where the transition also has a reset arc on that place, of the combined reset+output type of [EXP-013].

The export *shall* draw into each place on which a transition has a reset arc an edge from that transition or from one of its junctions, of type reset or, where the transition's output spec also names that place, of the combined reset+output type of [EXP-013].

**Acceptance Criteria:**
1. Export produces valid, parseable output in the chosen format.
2. All places and transitions in the net are represented.
3. All arcs (input, output, inhibitor, read, reset) are represented.

**Implementation notes:**
- Java: DOT (Graphviz) format
- TypeScript: DOT (Graphviz) format
- Rust: DOT (Graphviz) format

**Test derivation:** Build net with all arc types; export; verify output parses correctly.
acceptance: Export produces valid, parseable output in the chosen format.
All places and transitions in the net are represented.
All arcs (input, output, inhibitor, read, reset) are represented.

spans.label: s1

requirements.testDerivation: Export net; verify transition nodes use correct shape syntax.

spans.text: Transitions are rendered as rectangles or bars (following Petri net convention).
spans.label: s1

spans.text: Transition names are displayed as labels.
spans.label: s2

spans.label: s3

spans.label: s4

paragraphs.text: Transitions are rendered as rectangles or bars (following Petri net convention). Transition names are displayed as labels.

The transition category is the `transition` row of the node table in `spec/petri-net-styles.json`; its shape is `box`, a rectangle, so the export draws rectangles and does not use bars. No place row, no junction row and not the `interface-port` row has that shape. The `sync-channel` row is also `box`; a place node never has it, since [EXP-002] draws every place node with a place row. Transitions and places are therefore told apart by this requirement together with [EXP-002]. The timing interval and the priority that may follow the name in a transition's label are given by [EXP-007].
The export *shall* draw a node for every transition of the net.
The export *shall* draw no node that stands for a transition the net does not have.
The export *shall* give a node the transition category exactly when the node stands for a transition.
The export *shall* label the node of a transition with a text that starts with the transition's name as written in the net.
*Where* the configuration hides the timing interval and the priority, the export *shall* label the node of a transition with the transition's name alone.

requirements.title: Styling
requirements.testDerivation: Net with start and end places; export; verify styling applied.

spans.text: The export applies visual styling to distinguish node categories:
spans.label: s1

spans.text: The export *shall* give a terminal place the terminal category.
spans.label: s2

spans.text: The export *shall* give an environment place that is not a terminal place the environment category.
spans.label: s3

spans.text: The export *shall* give an ordinary place the start category exactly when no transition's output spec names it.
spans.label: s4

spans.label: s5

spans.label: s6

paragraphs.text: The export applies visual styling to distinguish node categories:

- **Start places** (no incoming arcs): highlighted (e.g., green)
- **End places** (no outgoing arcs): highlighted (e.g., blue)
- **Transitions**: distinct color (e.g., yellow)

Each place category names a row of the node table in `spec/petri-net-styles.json`: terminal, environment, start, end, or the regular `place` row. In this section an ordinary place is a place that is neither a terminal place ([EXEC-042]) nor an environment place ([ENV-001]). In the bullets above, an incoming arc of a place is an output arc on it (some transition's output spec names it), and an input arc on it is an outgoing arc; inhibitor arcs and reset arcs are neither, and whether a read arc is an outgoing arc is left open in this version (see the last two sentences below). The category of a place is the one the export's mapper gives it; a documentation generator that afterwards redraws the interface ports of a subnet body with the `interface-port` row ([EXP-011]) is outside this requirement.
The export *shall* give a terminal place the terminal category.
The export *shall* give an environment place that is not a terminal place the environment category.
